claims.text: An integrated machine-learning framework can predict optimal non-equiatomic compositional adjustments for low-dimensional high-entropy alloys.
Machine-learning-guided compositional adjustments can fine-tune local magnetic interactions and systematically enhance the magnetocaloric effect near a magnetic phase transition.
The initial low-dimensional non-equiatomic HEA is a disordered multielement solid solution.
The initial alloy has inherent compositional inhomogeneities.
The proposed model is trained jointly on high-fidelity computational simulations and existing experimental datasets.
DFT-based calculations incorporating longitudinal spin fluctuations can provide finite-temperature magnetic information for high-entropy alloys.
Machine learning can be integrated with DFT free-energy calculations for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The proposed model can identify targeted substitutions that balance ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic tendencies.
Subtle compositional adjustments modulate local magnetic ordering and exchange interactions.
Changing the relative concentrations of magnetic elements alters local magnetic exchange pathways.
Altered exchange pathways shift the balance between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions.
Shifting the balance between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions tunes the field-induced magnetic entropy change and enhances the magnetocaloric response.
The ML-optimized alloy will have a larger and more predictable magnetic entropy change near its magnetic transition than alloys tuned by traditional methods.
Traditional fixed-substitution schemes and equiatomic approximations do not fully exploit the multidimensional compositional landscape.
The proposed approach is expected to apply to low-dimensional HEAs near their magnetic phase transitions.
Results from the proposed approach may not extrapolate to bulk materials or temperatures far from the magnetic transition.
The enhancement magnitude is uncertain because of compositional inhomogeneities and dimensional constraints.

Failure of ML-selected samples to produce a statistically significant increase in magnetic entropy change relative to conventionally tuned controls under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
